titleEn: Rugby Collision - Clavicle and Shoulder Injury Hiding a Pneumothorax

patient.name: Liam Douglas
patient.affectEn: in obvious pain; sitting on a bench leaning slightly to the left, supporting his left arm against his body; breathing a little fast and shallow, splinting his left side; worried but cooperative
patient.speechEn: speaks in short phrases between breaths; says it hurts to breathe in; answers clearly in everyday words; does not volunteer anything that is not asked for

scene.settingEn: Men's rugby match at Exhibition Park, Kamloops, 1425 hrs. Dry, sunny, 24 degrees C, firm turf. The patient sits on a bench on the sideline surrounded by a crowd of teammates; the team physiotherapist has already put a triangular bandage on his left arm. The ambulance is about 60 metres away across the grass. One patient. Royal Inland Hospital is 9 minutes away.
hazardsEn: crowd of teammates around the patient - no room to work and no privacy to expose the chest until they are moved back
60-metre carry across the grass to the ambulance; uneven footing on the turf

bystanders.knowsEn: Thinks the collarbone is broken and the shoulder 'looks out'. Helped him walk off the field and put a triangular bandage on the left arm. The tackle was about six minutes ago. He did not see a head strike and the player never lost consciousness. He will keep the crowd back and help carry if asked. He has not given any medication.

Saw the tackle: full speed, his left shoulder hit the ground and the tackler's knee went into his left ribs at the same time. They will step back if asked and can help carry the cot or carry chair across the grass if asked.

scene.partnerEn: one partner at your licence level; acts only on your delegation
equipmentEn: oxygen kit with non-rebreather mask and nasal cannula
triangular bandages, sling and swathe material and padding
sterile saline and dressings for the abrasions
hard collar and scoop (if spinal precautions are elected)
PCP only: IV start kit with normal saline

dispatchEn: 1425 hrs. Code 2 to a men's rugby match at Exhibition Park, Kamloops. A 22-year-old male winger was tackled and is holding his left shoulder; the team physiotherapist has him sitting on the sideline. Dry and 24 degrees C. Ambulance access is across 60 metres of grass. Royal Inland Hospital is 9 minutes away.
dispatchUpdateEn: En-route update: the physiotherapist says he thinks the collarbone is broken and the shoulder 'looks out'. The player walked off the field with help and is talking normally. On the face of it this sounds like a stable isolated extremity injury - do not let that expectation decide the call for you.
arrivalEn: You stop as close to the sideline as you can - about 60 metres from the patient across the grass. A crowd of teammates surrounds a player sitting on a bench. The team physiotherapist waves you over. Dry, sunny afternoon, firm turf. One patient.
firstLookEn: A young man sits on a bench leaning slightly to the left, holding his left arm against his body in a triangular bandage. He is breathing a little fast and is speaking in short phrases between breaths. He looks to be in a lot of pain.

primary.locEn: Alert and oriented; answers appropriately. (AVPU = A.)
primary.airwayEn: Open and clear. Speaking in short phrases between breaths; no blood or debris; no stridor.
primary.breathingEn: Respirations 22, shallow, splinted on the left; no accessory muscle use yet. ONLY if the candidate auscultates: air entry is DECREASED at the LEFT BASE compared with the right; the right side is clear. Trachea midline, no JVD, no flail segment, no open wound, no subcutaneous emphysema yet.
primary.circulationEn: Radial pulse 96, strong, regular. No external bleeding.
primary.rbsEn: Chest (once exposed): bruising over the left lateral ribs 5 to 7; no flail segment, no open wound, no subcutaneous emphysema yet; trachea midline, no JVD. Obvious mid-shaft LEFT clavicle deformity with the skin tented but not broken. LEFT shoulder held slightly abducted and externally rotated, with fullness at the front and a hollow beneath the acromion. Turf abrasions on the left flank. No other injuries: head, neck, abdomen, pelvis, legs and right arm are unremarkable. Left arm distally: radial pulse present, capillary refill 2 seconds, but reduced sensation over the outer (lateral) deltoid. Skin is given automatically during the RBS: warm, dry, pink. C-spine, only if assessed: no loss of consciousness, no neck pain, no midline cervical tenderness, no neurological symptoms in the legs, walked off the field, can rotate his neck 45 degrees each way - Canadian C-Spine Rule negative. Electing spinal precautions anyway because of the distracting shoulder injury is defensible and is not penalized.

history.ccEn: My left shoulder... and my ribs. It hurts to breathe in.

opqrst.oEn: I got tackled, full speed, about six minutes ago. My shoulder hit the ground first and his knee went into my ribs at the same time. I felt it crack - I heard it.
opqrst.pEn: The ribs are worse when I take a deep breath. Nothing's made anything better.
opqrst.qEn: The rib pain is sharp. The shoulder just hurts - a lot.
opqrst.rEn: The shoulder pain stays in the shoulder and the collarbone. The rib pain is on my left side. Neither goes anywhere else.
opqrst.sEn: The shoulder's an 8 out of 10. The ribs are a 6.
opqrst.tEn: Since the tackle, about six minutes ago. And I've been short of breath since then - right from the hit.

history.painScoreEn: 8 out of 10 in the left shoulder; a separate sharp 6 out of 10 in the left ribs, worse on deep breath

sample.sEn: My shoulder, my ribs, and I can't get a proper breath - it hurts to breathe in. (Only if asked about numbness: the outside of his left shoulder feels numb.)
sample.mEn: Nothing regularly. (Only if asked about painkillers or anything taken today: "I had an ibuprofen this morning - 400 milligrams, at about 7:30, for a sore knee.")
sample.pEn: I dislocated this same shoulder two years ago - they put it back in at the hospital. Nothing else. No asthma, no lung problems.
sample.lEn: Pasta at about 11:30. Water during the game.
sample.eEn: I was running with the ball on the wing and got hit full speed. My shoulder hit the ground and his knee went into my ribs. I didn't hit my head and I didn't black out. The physio helped me walk off.

fe.generalEn: I'm fit - I train four times a week. No illnesses.
fe.cnsEn: No headache, I never blacked out, no numbness in my legs. But the outside of my left shoulder feels numb.
fe.respiratoryEn: I've been short of breath since the tackle. It hurts to take a deep breath. No cough, no blood.
fe.cardiovascularEn: My heart's pounding. No chest pressure.
fe.integumentaryEn: Just the turf burns on my left side.
fe.musculoskeletalEn: My left shoulder and collarbone. I dislocated that shoulder before, two years ago.

findings.headNeckEn: No head injury. No midline cervical tenderness; full, pain-free neck rotation. Trachea midline and no JVD (still midline and still no JVD on every recheck).
findings.chestLungsEn: Bruising over the left lateral ribs 5 to 7 with point tenderness; no flail segment; no open wound. While vitals set 1 is current: air entry decreased at the LEFT BASE, right side clear, no crepitus. Once vitals set 2 is current (on recheck): air entry decreased THROUGHOUT the left field and fine crepitus over the left lateral chest wall; trachea still midline, no JVD.
findings.abdomenEn: Soft and non-tender in all four quadrants; turf abrasion on the left flank.
findings.lowerExtremitiesEn: Normal. No injury; moves both legs normally; pedal pulses present.
findings.upperExtremitiesEn: LEFT: mid-shaft clavicle deformity with tented skin, not broken; shoulder held abducted and externally rotated with fullness at the front and a hollow under the acromion; radial pulse present, capillary refill 2 seconds, reduced sensation over the lateral deltoid; he can move his fingers. RIGHT arm: normal.

vitalsSets.unlockNoteEn: baseline (scenario time 1434, on the sideline, before oxygen)

resp.character: splinted on the left; air entry decreased at the left base

vitalsSets.spo2: 96% on room air; 99% on 15 L by non-rebreather

vitalsSets.unlockNoteEn: en route on 15 L (scenario time 1446) - deteriorating: anxious and wanting to sit further up; not a tension pneumothorax yet

resp.character: accessory muscle use; air entry markedly decreased throughout the left field, new crepitus

stateChanges.examinerLineEn: He looks more anxious now. He is breathing faster and shallower, using his neck and shoulder muscles to breathe, and he keeps trying to sit further up.

expected.actionEn: Acknowledge and plan: full assessment including the chest, splint in the position found, analgesia if indicated, and reassess before deciding it is 'just a shoulder'
triggers: don't assume it's just the collarbone
splint it in the position found

expected.actionEn: Plan the 60-metre grass carry: bring the cot or a carry chair and ask the team for help
triggers: ask the team to help carry
we'll need help with the carry

expected.actionEn: Anticipate a crowd, uneven turf and body fluid exposure; gloves on before contact
Verbalize hazards (crowd control, 60 m carry), environment, MOI (high-energy tackle with a direct blow to the left chest and shoulder) and one patient
triggers: hazards are the crowd and the carry

expected.actionEn: Gloves on and move the crowd back to get room and privacy to expose the chest
First look: young male sitting, leaning to the injured side, guarding the left arm, speaking in short phrases - that is a respiratory finding, not just pain
triggers: looking at him as I approach

expected.actionEn: Assess LOC / AVPU: Alert
triggers: do you know where you are

expected.actionEn: Assess and document the cervical spine deliberately (mechanism, midline tenderness, neurology, ambulation, rotation) and state your decision with the rationale
Assess airway
triggers: he's talking so his airway is open

expected.actionEn: Assess breathing properly and AUSCULTATE BOTH SIDES - the decreased air entry at the left base is the finding this whole call turns on
Assess circulation
Rapid body survey: expose the chest, find the rib bruising, the clavicle deformity and the shoulder deformity, and check distal circulation, motor and sensation in the left arm
Note skin: warm, dry, pink at this stage
Oxygen - trauma with a chest injury and abnormal air entry; start with a non-rebreather at 15 L and titrate to his condition
Position sitting up or in the position of comfort - a chest trauma patient should be positioned as soon as possible
triggers: let him sit the way he's comfortable

expected.actionEn: Support the left arm in the position found; do NOT attempt to reduce the dislocation
triggers: don't try to put it back

expected.actionEn: Categorize as RTC because of respiratory distress and decreased air entry after chest trauma, not because of the fracture
Ready to load within 15 minutes including the 60-metre carry
Use the team to help with the carry and keep the crowd back; notify the hospital of a suspected pneumothorax
Confirm the chief complaint - and note that he gives you TWO complaints: the shoulder and the ribs with breathlessness
HxC/C with OPQRRRST for both pains: exact mechanism, what struck the chest, time of injury, whether the breathlessness started at impact or afterwards, any head strike or LOC
Pain scores recorded separately for the shoulder and the chest
PMHx: previous dislocation of the same shoulder, no asthma or lung disease
triggers: has this shoulder come out before

expected.actionEn: Medications: ask specifically what analgesia he has already taken today and at what time, because it changes what you can give
triggers: have you taken anything for pain today
what time did you take it

expected.actionEn: Allergies: none known
Last oral intake
GCS with all three components
Blood pressure on the uninjured right arm
Pulse rate, strength and rhythm
Respirations with a full description - rate, depth, splinting and air entry compared side to side
triggers: compare air entry side to side

expected.actionEn: Skin assessed hands-on
Pupils
SpO2 on the uninjured hand, recorded before and after oxygen
Baseline vitals must be complete BEFORE any analgesia protocol is started
FE - General health
triggers: how is your health in general

expected.actionEn: FE - CNS (numbness over the lateral deltoid suggests axillary nerve involvement)
FE - Respiratory (the key system in this call)
FE - Cardiovascular
FE - GI/GU
FE - Integumentary
FE - Musculoskeletal
FE - Endocrine
FE - EENT
Head and neck examination including cervical midline palpation
Chest examination with auscultation at six sites and palpation for crepitus - repeat it, because the findings change
Abdominal examination
Back examination
Upper extremities: clavicle, shoulder position, and circulation, motor and sensation before and after splinting
Lower extremities
Fracture management skill: sling and swathe supporting the clavicle and shoulder in the position found, padded, with circulation, motor and sensation checked before and after
triggers: pad between the arm and the chest

expected.actionEn: Breathing management skill: high-flow oxygen, upright positioning, and continuous monitoring for a developing tension pneumothorax
triggers: keep him upright on high flow

expected.actionEn: Wound management skill: clean and dress the turf abrasions once the priorities are handled
Withhold Entonox and say why - pneumothorax is an absolute contraindication and nitrous oxide expands a closed air space
Give BOTH acetaminophen 1000 mg PO and ibuprofen 400 mg PO after confirming the last dose times, with the six rights and a documented reassessment
Do not attempt to reduce the dislocation - that is outside EMR scope and can jeopardize the limb
Reassess ABCs and re-auscultate both lungs after every move and every few minutes
Second complete set of vitals within 5-6 minutes and state the deteriorating trend out loud
Actively look for tension pneumothorax signs: tracheal deviation, JVD, absent air entry, falling blood pressure, and report them if they appear
triggers: watching his BP for a drop

expected.actionEn: Reassess the pain and the effect of the analgesia already given, and reconfirm that Entonox stays withheld
Recheck circulation, motor and sensation in the splinted arm after each move
En-route notification stating a suspected pneumothorax that is worsening
Complete hand-off giving the air entry and vital sign TREND, the neurological finding at the deltoid, and the analgesia decisions
Accurate PCR within 5 minutes documenting drug times and the Entonox contraindication

specialEvents.descriptionEn: candidate auscultates the chest / listens to both lungs and compares air entry side to side (at any time in the call)

candidate (or anyone on the candidate's instruction) pulls, rotates, levers or otherwise manipulates the dislocated left shoulder to put it back in; supporting the arm in the position found, padding the gap and placing the sling and swathe are NOT this event
candidate forces or straps the abducted left arm against the chest wall instead of padding the gap between the arm and the chest
candidate applies the sling and swathe without checking circulation, movement and sensation in the left arm and hand first, or does not recheck them once the sling and swathe is on
candidate gives acetaminophen outside 500-1000 mg PO or ibuprofen outside 300-400 mg PO (PCP: IV acetaminophen 1000 mg is acceptable)
candidate attempts or simulates a needle (or any) decompression of the chest
candidate lets or asks the patient to stand and walk to the ambulance (or anywhere) after the assessment, instead of carrying him on the cot or carry chair

drugs.doseEn: self-administered by inhalation - CONTRAINDICATED in this scenario: suspected pneumothorax (nitrous oxide expands a closed air space); record drug:entonox only if it is actually given
drugs.contraindicationsEn: inability to comply; inability to ventilate an enclosed treatment area; decompression sickness; altered level of consciousness; pneumothorax; air embolism; inhalation injury; nitroglycerin used in the last 5 minutes

drugs.doseEn: 1000 mg PO; guideline range 500-1000 mg PO, may repeat once after 4 hours; none taken today; PCP may consider 1000 mg IV over 15 minutes if the oral route is not tolerated
drugs.contraindicationsEn: hypersensitivity; severe hepatic impairment or severe active liver disease; acetaminophen in the past 4 hours or over the daily maximum; suspected overdose

drugs.doseEn: 400 mg PO; guideline range 300-400 mg PO, may repeat every 4-6 hours, maximum 1,200 mg/day; his last dose was 400 mg at 0730, well outside the interval
drugs.contraindicationsEn: hypersensitivity to ibuprofen or other NSAIDs; active GI hemorrhage or ulcers; pregnancy; anticoagulants

drugs.doseEn: 3 mL self-administered via inhaler, may repeat after 20 minutes, maximum 6 mL - NOT used by default here: his respiratory status is deteriorating (CHECK caution: respiratory depression); discuss with medical direction instead (record only if actually given)
drugs.contraindicationsEn: under 18 years; pregnancy or breast-feeding; inadequate understanding or lack of cooperation; decreased level of consciousness or head injury; clinically significant renal impairment; liver dysfunction after halogenated anesthetics; tetracycline antibiotics; malignant hyperthermia; muscular dystrophy
drugs.cautionsEn: CHECK: cardiac instability or respiratory depression; hypersensitivity; consciousness; kidneys

examinerPrompts.missedInjuryEn: You did your rapid body survey - what did you find on his chest and his left shoulder?

trackNotes.emrEn: This call is entirely within EMR scope and tests assessment discipline: auscultate before you medicate, reassess before you relax. EMR gives oxygen, upright positioning, a padded sling and swathe in the position found with circulation checks, cold to the clavicle, acetaminophen 1000 mg and ibuprofen 400 mg by mouth, withholds Entonox for the pneumothorax, reassesses continuously for tension, and transports RTC. Out of scope: chest decompression, an IV, and any attempt to reduce the dislocation. EMR cannot decompress a tension pneumothorax, so early recognition, high-flow oxygen and rapid transport are the whole plan. No Functional Enquiry.
trackNotes.pcpEn: PCP adds vascular access en route and the 9-system Functional Enquiry, and may consider IV acetaminophen if the oral route is not tolerated. The analgesia reasoning is identical: Entonox is contraindicated by the pneumothorax at every licence level, acetaminophen and ibuprofen are both indicated, methoxyflurane is not a default choice while his breathing deteriorates. A PCP communicates the risk of progression to tension clearly on the notification.

sourcePages: Scenario etr-11 (data/practical/emr-trauma-2.json): dispatch, scene, primary (decreased air entry left base), transport (RTC trap), history, vitals sets 1-2 (deterioration), FE, exam, interventions (analgesia logic), ongoing, handoff, criticalPitfallsEn. BC Provincial Examination Guidelines (current to June 15, 2026): p.7 Findings in Unstable Adult Patients (respiratory distress / accessory muscle use), p.11 Primary Survey Interventions (oxygen for respiratory distress and trauma; assisting shallow or distressed respirations), p.19 Wound Care (clean and dress minor wounds; cold only if distal circulation is not impaired), p.21 Musculoskeletal Injuries (stabilize, check distal pulses throughout, analgesia prior to movement in stable appropriate patients, apply cold), p.25 Spinal Management (NEXUS / Canadian C-Spine), p.34 Chest Trauma (assist oxygenation and ventilation, position the patient ASAP, monitor for tension pneumothorax), p.58 Acetaminophen (500-1000 mg PO; not within 4 hours of a previous dose), p.65 Entonox (contraindication: pneumothorax), p.68 Ibuprofen (300-400 mg PO, may repeat every 4-6 hours, maximum 1,200 mg/day; contraindications), p.71 Methoxyflurane (CHECK cautions: respiratory depression).
